water.headline: Every time you use AI, it uses a bottle of water.

keyWord.explanation: The researchers’ estimate was about half a liter of water for every 10–50 answers, not a bottle for each use, and it rested on guesses about cooling and power.

water.scoreReason: The headline treats a computer estimate as if someone measured it, and turns a bottle for every 10–50 answers into a bottle for every single use.

W1.reason: “Guzzling” adds drama the evidence doesn't need.

claimDial.text: AI data centers are guzzling the water in America's dry towns.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

P2.reason: Talks about all dry towns, when the evidence covers some places.

W1.reason: “Guzzling” adds drama the evidence doesn't need.

claimDial.text: Every time you use AI, it uses a bottle of water.
claimDial.origin: headline claim

claimDial.text: AI is greedily drinking America dry and will leave us all without water.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

P1.reason: States as fact something no evidence shows.

P2.reason: Stretches local strain to the whole country.

P3.reason: Tells a guess about the future as a sure thing.

W1.reason: “Drinking America dry” is alarm, not evidence.

W2.reason: Treats AI as greedy, when companies decide where to build.

finePrint.label: Fact: Not all data centers are used for AI.
finePrint.text: Data centers also run email, websites, video streaming and online storage. Most numbers about data center water use add all of these together, so only part of that water goes to AI.

finePrint.label: Fact: Newer estimates are much smaller.
finePrint.text: In August 2025, Google estimated that a typical text question to its Gemini AI uses about 0.26 milliliters of water, or about five drops. That’s the company’s own estimate, and no one outside has checked it.

finePrint.label: Fact: Some of the water goes back.
finePrint.text: Data centers take water from rivers, lakes and wells, and some of it is returned. The water that evaporates while cooling the machines is what a town actually loses.

finePrint.label: Fact: Hot days matter most.
finePrint.text: A data center can use little water over a whole year but a lot on the hottest days, which is exactly when a town’s water is scarcest.

quiz.statement: Every time you use AI, it uses a bottle of water.
quiz.why: The study behind the bottle figure estimated one bottle for every 10 to 50 answers from an older model, not one per use. Google’s own estimate for a typical question today is about five drops. Both are estimates, not measurements.

quiz.statement: A data center can strain a town’s water on hot days, even if its yearly use looks small.
quiz.why: Data centers use the most water for cooling on the hottest days, which is also when everyone else needs water most.

quiz.statement: If your town has water restrictions, AI data centers are the cause.
quiz.why: Not necessarily. Water restrictions usually come from drought and from everyone in the area using more water. Public records rarely show that one user, like a data center, caused them.

water.carefulHeadline: AI data centers threaten water supplies in some dry US towns.
water.carefulScoreReason: The more careful version says “threaten” and talks only about some places, which matches what the evidence shows.
water.headlineSource: Claim tracked from Windows Central, a tech news site, which made it in a September 2023 headline: “Bing Chat and ChatGPT use ‘1 bottle of water’ in cooling for every query, leading to concerns for local water supplies.”
water.carefulSource: Our wording, based on a 2025 Bloomberg investigation into where AI data centers get their water.
water.headlineSourceLinkText: Bing Chat and ChatGPT use ‘1 bottle of water’ in cooling for every query, leading to concerns for local water supplies

jobs.headline: AI will take all our jobs.

keyWord.explanation: Even Musk said “probably”. The evidence shows AI changing tasks and slowing hiring for some young workers, not replacing every job.

jobs.scoreReason: The headline turns Musk's “probably” into a sure thing, and jumps from some tasks AI can do to every job.

claimDial.origin: careful version

claimDial.text: AI could wipe out half of US entry-level office jobs by about 2030.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

W1.reason: “Wipe out” adds drama to an expert's warning.

claimDial.text: AI will wipe out half of US entry-level office jobs by 2030.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

P3.reason: Turns an expert's “could” into a sure thing.

W1.reason: “Wipe out” adds drama to an expert's warning.

claimDial.text: AI will take all our jobs.
claimDial.origin: headline claim

claimDial.text: AI is already destroying jobs everywhere and will soon want every single one.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

P1.reason: Says jobs are already being destroyed everywhere, which the data don't show.

P2.reason: Stretches some tasks to every job.

P3.reason: Tells a guess about the future as a sure thing.

W2.reason: Says AI “wants” jobs, when employers make those choices.

finePrint.label: Fact: Musk said “probably”.
finePrint.text: At a Paris tech conference in May 2024, Elon Musk said: “Probably none of us will have a job.” He added that work could become optional, like a hobby.

finePrint.label: Fact: A job “exposed” to AI isn’t a job at risk.
finePrint.text: “Exposed” means AI could help with or do some of the tasks in a job. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics says it doesn’t measure your chance of losing your job.

finePrint.label: Fact: So far, it’s fewer hires, not mass layoffs.
finePrint.text: Where a change shows up, it’s mainly that fewer young people are being hired into jobs where AI can do a lot of the work.

finePrint.label: Fact: Young workers in AI-heavy jobs are losing ground.
finePrint.text: In August 2026, the number of 22- to 25-year-olds working in the jobs where AI can do the most tasks was 4.4% lower than a year earlier. In the jobs where AI can do the fewest tasks, it was 2.0% lower. These figures come from ADP, a payroll company, and don’t prove AI caused the drop.

finePrint.label: Fact: The scariest warning is a forecast.
finePrint.text: In May 2025, the head of Anthropic, a company that sells AI, warned that AI could wipe out half of entry-level office jobs within one to five years. That’s a prediction, not something that has happened.

quiz.why: Not proven. Even Musk said “probably”, and so far there’s no sign of jobs disappearing across the whole economy.

quiz.statement: Fewer young people are being hired into jobs where AI can do a lot of the work.
quiz.why: Payroll data studied by ADP and Stanford researchers show employment of 22- to 25-year-olds falling faster in those jobs, mostly because fewer are being hired.

quiz.statement: Researchers have proven that AI caused that drop.
quiz.why: No. The researchers say their findings show a pattern, not a cause. Other things, like education and trends that started before AI, could also play a part.

jobs.carefulHeadline: AI could eliminate half of US entry-level office jobs by about 2030.
jobs.carefulScoreReason: The more careful version says “could”, and it's an expert's educated guess about the future, though nobody has been able to test the half-of-jobs number yet.
jobs.headlineSource: Claim tracked from Elon Musk, who made it at a tech conference in Paris in May 2024. CNN's headline was “Elon Musk says AI will take all our jobs.”
jobs.carefulSource: Our wording, based on a May 2025 warning by Dario Amodei, head of the AI company Anthropic.
jobs.headlineSourceLinkText: Elon Musk says AI will take all our jobs

energy-climate.headline: AI will make climate change worse.

keyWord.explanation: “Will” makes it sound certain. How much AI adds depends on how fast its power use grows and how clean the electricity gets, and its possible climate benefits haven’t been proven or ruled out.

energy-climate.scoreReason: AI's growing power use is adding emissions, so “worse” has a real basis. But “will” sounds surer than the evidence, which says it depends on how clean the power gets.

claimDial.text: AI's growing power use could raise US carbon emissions by 2030.
claimDial.origin: careful version

claimDial.text: AI will make climate change worse.
AI's exploding power use will raise US carbon emissions by 2030.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

P3.reason: Turns “could” into a sure thing, though it depends on how power is made.

W1.reason: “Exploding” adds drama to a fast but measured rise.

claimDial.text: AI will only intensify climate change.
claimDial.origin: The Nation’s original headline (December 2025), scored with the same checks

P1.reason: “Only” treats it as established that AI has no offsetting climate benefits. The IEA describes possible efficiency and climate benefits as conditional: neither proven nor ruled out.

P2.reason: Global scope matches the global data-center evidence; no distinct scope problem.

P3.reason: States a certain outcome. The IEA says the effect depends on demand growth, efficiency and how the electricity is generated, and clean-energy investment is also growing.

W1.reason: No distinct additional problem; the issue is scored once above.

W2.reason: No human-like agency is attributed to AI.

claimDial.text: AI is single-handedly destroying the planet and will make climate change unstoppable.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

P1.reason: States as fact something no evidence shows.

P2.reason: Blames AI alone for a planet-wide problem.

P3.reason: Tells a guess about the future as a sure thing.

W1.reason: “Destroying the planet” is alarm, not evidence.

W2.reason: Treats AI as the one acting, when people choose how to power it.

finePrint.label: Fact: Using electricity isn’t the same as polluting.
finePrint.text: Whether AI’s electricity harms the climate depends on how it’s made. Power from wind, sun or nuclear plants adds little pollution; power from coal or gas adds more.

finePrint.label: Fact: AI is only part of data centers’ electricity use.
finePrint.text: All US data centers together used 4.4% of the country’s electricity in 2023, according to Berkeley Lab. That includes email, websites and streaming, not just AI.

finePrint.label: Fact: Buying green power doesn’t mean using it every hour.
finePrint.text: A company can buy enough renewable power to cover a whole year, but at night or on still days its data centers may still run on power from coal or gas.

finePrint.label: Fact: Data centers’ electricity use is expected to double.
finePrint.text: The International Energy Agency estimates data centers worldwide used 485 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025 and expects about 950 by 2030. That includes work that isn’t AI.

finePrint.label: Fact: AI might help the climate, but that isn’t proven.
finePrint.text: AI could cut pollution in other ways, like running power grids more efficiently. No one has shown those savings will outweigh the pollution from its own electricity.

quiz.statement: If a company buys enough renewable power over a year, its AI runs on clean power every hour.
quiz.why: Buying a year’s worth of green power doesn’t mean clean power at every hour. At night or on still days, its data centers may run on power from coal or gas.

quiz.statement: US climate pollution could go down overall while AI still adds to it.
quiz.why: If cleaner power cuts pollution elsewhere, the total can fall even while AI’s extra electricity use pushes it up.

quiz.statement: It’s been proven that AI’s climate benefits cancel out its pollution.
quiz.why: Not proven. The savings depend on how widely AI is used for climate work, and using more AI also uses more electricity.

energy-climate.carefulHeadline: AI's growing power use could raise US carbon emissions by 2030.
energy-climate.carefulScoreReason: The more careful version says “could”, and there's a clear way it can happen: more demand for electricity, partly met by gas power plants.
energy-climate.headlineSource: Claim tracked from historian Juan Cole, who made it in a December 2025 article in The Nation headlined “AI Will Only Intensify Climate Change. The Tech Moguls Don’t Care.”
energy-climate.carefulSource: Our wording, based on a 2025 Cornell University study of the AI data center boom's environmental impact.
energy-climate.headlineSourceLinkText: AI Will Only Intensify Climate Change. The Tech Moguls Don’t Care.

creativity.headline: AI art is theft.

keyWord.explanation: Theft is a legal and moral judgment. US courts haven’t settled whether training AI on others’ work is legal, and one court found a specific use fair.

creativity.scoreReason: Artists really weren't asked before their work was used to train AI. But “theft” is a crime word, and it treats a question courts haven't settled as a fact.

claimDial.text: AI can reproduce copyrighted work from its training data.
claimDial.origin: careful version

claimDial.text: AI can spit out copies of copyrighted work it was trained on.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

W1.reason: “Spit out” adds drama to what tests found.

claimDial.text: AI art is theft.
claimDial.origin: headline claim

claimDial.text: AI art is stolen art, copied straight from real artists.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

P1.reason: States as fact that AI art is copied, which hasn't been shown.

P2.reason: Says all AI art, when copying has only been shown in targeted tests.

W1.reason: No extra drama beyond the copying claim already scored.

W2.reason: Doesn't say AI wants or plans anything.

claimDial.text: AI is a plagiarism machine that steals every artist's work and will kill human creativity.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

P1.reason: States wrongdoing as settled, when courts haven't decided.

P3.reason: Tells a guess about the future as a sure thing.

W1.reason: “Plagiarism machine” is a label, not evidence.

W2.reason: Says AI “steals”, when companies choose what to train on.

finePrint.label: Fact: Many artists weren’t asked.
finePrint.text: In 2022, Midjourney’s founder said the company didn’t ask living artists for permission before training its AI on their images.

finePrint.label: Fact: Training on art and copying art are separate questions.
finePrint.text: Using artwork to teach an AI is one legal question. The AI later producing a copy of that artwork is another.

finePrint.label: Fact: An artist’s style isn’t protected by copyright.
finePrint.text: Copying an artist’s style usually isn’t against the law. Copying their actual work can be.

finePrint.label: Fact: Legal doesn’t always mean fair.
finePrint.text: Even if a court says training AI on someone’s work is legal, that doesn’t settle whether artists should be asked or paid.

finePrint.label: Fact: Some artists are losing work.
finePrint.text: On one global freelance website, job posts for making images fell about 17% after AI image tools appeared, compared with jobs AI can’t do. That’s one website, not the whole US.

quiz.statement: Copying an artist’s style is against copyright law.
quiz.why: Usually not. Copyright protects specific works, not a style. Copying an actual artwork can break the law.

quiz.statement: Researchers have gotten AI chatbots to repeat long passages from books.
quiz.why: In 2025 tests, researchers got near word-for-word passages from books out of four popular AI models, including OpenAI’s GPT-4.1 and Google’s Gemini. It took special prompts, and sometimes getting around safety rules.

quiz.statement: A US court has ruled that AI art is theft.
quiz.why: No US court has ruled that. In a 2025 case about books, a judge said using books to train AI was fair use, but keeping pirated copies wasn’t. The company, Anthropic, later agreed to pay $1.5 billion.

creativity.carefulHeadline: AI can reproduce copyrighted work from its training data.
creativity.carefulScoreReason: The more careful version says “can”, and experiments have shown that it happens.
creativity.headlineSource: Claim tracked from researcher Trystan S. Goetze, who made it in the title of a 2024 research paper, “AI Art is Theft: Labour, Extraction, and Exploitation.”
creativity.carefulSource: Our wording, based on research showing AI models can repeat long passages from the work they were trained on.
creativity.headlineSourceLinkText: AI Art is Theft: Labour, Extraction, and Exploitation

privacy.headline: ChatGPT is sharing your secrets.

keyWord.explanation: “Sharing” suggests other people see your chats. What OpenAI describes is using chats to train its models, which you can turn off, plus limited access by staff for things like safety.

privacy.scoreReason: The headline calls training “sharing”, treats every chat as a secret, and ignores the settings that change what happens.

claimDial.origin: careful version

claimDial.text: ChatGPT may hoover up your personal chats to train its AI, depending on your settings.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

claimDial.text: ChatGPT hoovers up your personal chats to train its AI.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

P2.reason: Drops “depending on your settings”, so it sounds like every chat.

W1.reason: “Hoover up” adds drama to what the policy says.

P1.reason: States as fact something no evidence shows.

P3.reason: Tells a guess about the future as a sure thing.

finePrint.label: Fact: Training, storing and sharing are three different things.
finePrint.text: Training means your chats help improve the AI. Storing means OpenAI keeps your chats. Sharing means someone else can see them. Each has its own settings and rules.

finePrint.label: Fact: Turning off training doesn’t delete your chats.
finePrint.text: Your chats stay saved until you delete them. Even then, OpenAI can keep some for legal or security reasons.

finePrint.label: Fact: Temporary Chats are kept for up to 30 days.
finePrint.text: They aren’t used for training, but OpenAI keeps them for up to 30 days for safety checks. If you save one, it becomes a normal chat.

finePrint.label: Fact: Anyone with a shared link can see that chat.
finePrint.text: If you share a chat by link, anyone who has the link can read it. Deleting the link doesn’t remove copies people already saved.

finePrint.label: Fact: Your privacy rights depend on where you live.
finePrint.text: Californians have the legal right to see, correct and delete the personal data companies hold about them. Not every American has those rights.

quiz.statement: Turning off training deletes my old chats.
quiz.why: Training and storage are separate settings. To remove chats, you have to delete them.

quiz.statement: A thumbs-up or thumbs-down you give can still be used for training, even if you’ve turned training off.
quiz.why: OpenAI says feedback you send is an exception to turning training off.

quiz.statement: Other ChatGPT users can read my chats.
quiz.why: Not unless you share a link to a chat. Some OpenAI staff and outside companies it works with can see chats for specific reasons, like safety checks.

options.label: Personal account, training setting on
options.result: May be used to train OpenAI's models. Saved until you delete it.

options.label: Personal account, training setting off
options.result: Not used for training, except feedback you send with thumbs up or down. Still saved until you delete it.

options.label: Temporary Chat
options.result: Not used for training. Kept for up to 30 days for safety checks, then removed unless you save it.

options.label: Business or Enterprise account
options.result: Not used for training by default. Your organization controls who can see chats and how long they're kept.

privacy.carefulHeadline: ChatGPT may use your personal-account chats to train its AI, depending on your settings.
privacy.carefulScoreReason: The more careful version says “may” and “depending on your settings”, which matches what OpenAI's own policy says.
privacy.headlineSource: Claim tracked from Tom's Guide, a tech advice website, which made it in an April 2023 headline: “ChatGPT is sharing your secrets — keep your chats private by changing this setting.”
privacy.carefulSource: Our wording, based on OpenAI's own privacy settings, as explained by Tom's Guide.
privacy.headlineSourceLinkText: ChatGPT is sharing your secrets — keep your chats private by changing this setting

existential-risk.headline: AI will kill us all.

keyWord.explanation: Stated as a certainty, about all AI. The evidence shows real reasons for concern about future, much smarter AI, not that extinction is guaranteed.

existential-risk.scoreReason: The headline talks about all AI, drops the authors' own condition about how a super-smart AI gets built, and says as a certainty that everyone will die. That's the most extreme claim there is, so it goes off the charts.

claimDial.text: Future AI much smarter than people could pose serious risks, and experts disagree about how big they are.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

claimDial.text: Building superintelligent AI with 2025-era methods will kill everyone on Earth.
claimDial.origin: careful version

claimDial.text: Superintelligent AI built with today's methods will decide to kill us all.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

P3.reason: Tells a guess about the future as a sure thing.

W2.reason: Says AI would “decide” to kill us; the authors' worry is about goals, not intent.

claimDial.text: AI could easily wipe out humanity within a few years.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

P1.reason: A prediction, not a claim that it has already happened.

P2.reason: Says all AI, when the worry is about future super-smart AI.

P3.reason: “Easily” and “within a few years” are far surer than experts are.

W1.reason: Plainly says what it predicts, without extra drama.

W2.reason: Doesn't say AI wants or plans anything.

claimDial.text: AI will kill us all.
claimDial.origin: headline claim

finePrint.label: Fact: The claim comes from a 2025 book.
finePrint.text: Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares make the case in their book If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies.

finePrint.label: Fact: The book is about “superintelligence”, not today’s chatbots.
finePrint.text: That means AI more capable than all of humanity combined. Nothing like that exists yet.

finePrint.label: Fact: The worry isn’t that AI hates us.
finePrint.text: The authors fear AI chasing its own goals and grabbing resources in ways that destroy what people need to survive.

finePrint.label: Fact: There are different kinds of AI risk.
finePrint.text: Everyone dying, a disaster that kills many people, people using AI to do harm, and losing control of AI are separate fears, with separate evidence.

finePrint.label: Fact: AI has misbehaved in tests.
finePrint.text: In made-up company scenarios, AI models blackmailed people (Anthropic, 2025). In UK government tests, AI agents tried things they weren’t allowed to do, and during skills tests, AI agents hacked a real website (2026). The made-up scenarios hurt no one, and the UK attempts failed.

quiz.statement: AI systems have done things in tests that their makers didn’t intend.
quiz.why: Anthropic, the UK’s AI Security Institute and the research group METR have all documented it.

quiz.statement: Experts agree on how likely it is that AI wipes out humanity.
quiz.why: The 2026 International AI Safety Report, written by experts from many countries, found wide disagreement about how likely it is and how soon.

quiz.statement: The risks from AI are all made up.
quiz.why: The incidents in tests are real, even though they don’t prove AI will wipe us out.

existential-risk.carefulHeadline: Building superintelligent AI with 2025-era methods will kill everyone on Earth.
existential-risk.carefulScoreReason: The more careful version keeps the authors' condition, but “will” still sounds surer than the evidence allows.
existential-risk.headlineSource: Claim tracked from AI-risk researchers Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares, who made it in the title of their 2025 book, “If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies.”
existential-risk.carefulSource: Our wording of the full argument in Yudkowsky and Soares's book, which applies it to AI built with today's methods.

earlierSource.label: An earlier version
earlierSource.text: Before the book, Yudkowsky wrote in TIME in March 2023, in an essay titled “Pausing AI Developments Isn't Enough. We Need to Shut it All Down,” that if anyone builds superhumanly smart AI under current conditions, “literally everyone on Earth will die.”
earlierSource.linkText: Pausing AI Developments Isn't Enough. We Need to Shut it All Down

existential-risk.headlineSourceLinkText: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies
